It is not about where they are now but about how far they have come and the trajectory of where they are headed. Extreme Poverty Rates: The share of the population living under the international extreme poverty threshold ($1.90/day) dropped from 43.3% in 1985 down to 5.3% by 2023  ). The national poverty headcount ratio similarly fell to 15.5% in 2025. Adult Literacy Rate: The overall literacy rate among adults expanded from 83.3% in 1980 to 98.5% in 2020.  Youth literacy (ages 15–24) currently sits above 99.7%. Child Mortality: The under-5 mortality rate dropped substantially from roughly 56 deaths per 1,000 live births in the mid-1980s to 27 per 1,000 live births by 2023 
Life Expectancy: Average life expectancy at birth rose from 62.7 years in 1985 to 70.1 years in recent estimates.

I understand the strength of this life of extreme poverty. Although I have not experienced this level of poverty life I’ve lived and have experienced a form of poverty life. I’ve learned at a very young age there is no sense with life experience comparisons, for me at the end of the day it is still poverty. Like so many others globally many of us was born in the life of poverty. Unless the child is exposed only to poverty, that child will only know poverty. As mentioned a child from this poverty life was asked “how long have you been here?”, Child replied “from birth”. I was raised in filipino home along with their family’s religion, and cultural ways of the Philippines. Filipino people are religious, very hard working. The very one thing that was very important in the home where I was being raised was respect, and cleanliness. I was not only the youngest in this filipino home, I also was the only boy growing up with and amongst 7 girls. At the time the ages of all the girls (my sisters) were 7, thru 15 years old. I justed made 6 years old in July before I was placed in this home in August 1969. Unless that child who was born in tunnel under country’s very busy freeway in philippines is told and hopefully shown of what is out in the world that very child will never know anything else. Life is already extremely fragile child’s mother will teach her child the utmost important things in their lives, basically all things to do to survive. Any other subject than survival is sort of bonus. When it came to people stopping by our home to visit weather it was family, or friends, business people, my foster parents were always nice always  making sure the visitors were comfortable. Constantly always being attentive to the visitors. If I was born and grew up in this life of poverty in the Philippines with being utmost truthful, honest, my behavior and thoughts would stem from what my upbringing would be like. Like every thing in life unless You’ve actually been born there, or experienced that level of poverty life most people answers will be in a most likely or a probability state. They keys to breaking the life-cycle of poverty, abuse, government housing, hood-life takes more than just 1 key, although it doesn’t have to take lots of keys. Key No.1: Faith, Prayer (it is very important to have faith, surely don’t hurt to pray) No.2: Information, Education (school, not always school necessarily), Key No.3: Options, Select, Choice, (making a 2 column list of Do’s and Don’t. Like to do, Do  not like to do), Key No.4: The Plan. Bottom line, I believe the main problem is overpopulation. When families have too many children, more houses need to be built to accommodate the growing population. More children may end up spending time on the streets, families have to buy more food and other necessities, and this can also lead to more waste and garbage.

When a father struggles to provide for a large family, he may sometimes be pushed into criminal activities just to make ends meet. The mother may have to work multiple jobs, leaving the children without proper supervision. In some communities, particularly informal settlements, these problems can become more serious.

There should be regular saturation drives and enforcement operations in informal-settlement areas in Tondo, under bridges, in Parañaque, and throughout Metro Manila. Authorities should monitor illegal dumping, apprehend people involved in drug-related crimes, and address theft, snatching, and other violent crimes.

It is also much more difficult for a family to provide adequately for three or more children. To be honest, Metro Manila already feels too small and overcrowded for families with five or more members.

If the Philippines were to consider a **one-child policy**, perhaps within 10 years we could gradually begin to see a decline in population growth and some positive effects on housing, transportation, employment, food supply, and waste management.

I also believe the government should have a serious discussion about the **death penalty for the most serious crimes**, although this should be considered separately from population control because capital punishment should be based on justice and public safety, not on reducing the population.
